title: The Song at the Boardwalk
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 1 of 40
content:
The first thing I noticed about Beach City was that the ocean did not care what I had left behind.

It rolled against the shore with the same patient rhythm, lifting silver foam and drawing it back into itself. It did not ask why I had arrived with one overstuffed suitcase, a backpack that pinched my shoulder, and a phone full of unanswered messages. It did not ask whether I had a plan. It simply kept breathing beneath the afternoon sun.

I stood at the edge of the boardwalk and let the wind tangle my hair. Somewhere behind me, a child laughed. A gull cried from the roof of a snack stand. The smell of salt, fried dough, and hot pavement settled around me like an unfamiliar blanket.

“You look like somebody who got lost on purpose.”

The voice came from my left. It was warm and rough around the edges, the kind of voice that had spent years singing in small rooms and larger ones, always without losing the ability to sound close. I turned and found a man sitting on the low sea wall with an acoustic guitar balanced across his knee.

Greg Universe looked exactly like someone who would speak to a stranger on a boardwalk. His hair was silver, his beard neatly untidy, and his faded T-shirt advertised a band I vaguely recognized from a record collection I had not opened in months. His smile was easy, but his eyes were observant. He had noticed the suitcase. He had noticed the way I kept checking the street behind me.

I glanced at the water. “Does it show?”

“Only if you’re looking.”

“And are you?”

“I’m a musician. We’re professionally nosy.” He gave the guitar a thoughtful strum. “Also, I’ve been sitting here for twenty minutes waiting for a chord to tell me what it wants to be. It hasn’t. I’m bored.”

That startled a laugh out of me. It felt rusty, as though it had been sitting in a drawer with the rest of the things I had not used lately.

Greg’s expression softened when he heard it. “There it is.”

“There what is?”

“Proof you’re not a ghost.”

The answer should have been ridiculous. Instead, it landed somewhere under my ribs, gentle and inconvenient. I adjusted the strap of my backpack and looked down at my suitcase. The wheel had collected a ribbon of sand, and one of the zippers had begun to open itself.

“I’m looking for a place to stay,” I admitted.

Greg tilted his head. “In Beach City?”

“That’s the idea.”

“You have a place lined up?”

I gave him a look.

“Right,” he said. “That was a silly question. Sorry.” He set the guitar aside and stood, moving with the careful looseness of somebody who had learned which joints complained before they actually did. “There’s a motel on the other side of town. It’s clean enough if you don’t look directly at the curtains.”

“That is a powerful endorsement.”

“I contain multitudes.”

He offered his hand, then paused before touching me. “Greg.”

I gave him my name, or rather, the name I used when I did not have the energy to explain the history of any other one. His handshake was brief and warm. He let go immediately, as if he understood that a stranger did not owe him more contact than they had offered.

“Nice to meet you,” he said. “Do you need help with the suitcase?”

The question nearly made me say no. I was accustomed to no meaning no, but I was also accustomed to people asking only so they could insist afterward. Greg waited without leaning toward the handle.

“Maybe,” I said.

“Excellent. I’m very good at maybe.”

He took the suitcase when I nodded. Not before. The wheel bumped over the uneven boards, and Greg lifted the bag over the worst cracks while I walked beside him. He did not fill the silence with questions. He pointed out a bakery with cinnamon rolls the size of saucers, a record shop that stayed open too late, and a little wash-and-fold place where the owner would let me use the phone if mine died.

“You know everyone here?” I asked.

“Not everyone. Just the people who have forgiven me for being late.”

“That sounds like a large group.”

“It’s a work in progress.”

The motel was exactly as advertised. The curtains were technically clean, the ice machine made a noise like a distressed animal, and the front desk clerk looked at my suitcase with the exhausted sympathy of someone who had seen many people arrive without a plan.

Greg set the bag down. “I can leave you here.”

I looked through the glass doors at the narrow lobby, then back at him. The ocean was still visible between the buildings, bright and indifferent. The thought of sitting alone in a room with one bed and no familiar object except my phone made my throat tighten.

Greg noticed. Of course he did.

“Or,” he said, “I know a diner where the coffee is bad but the pancakes are honest. You can eat, charge your phone, and decide whether you want to fight the curtains tonight.”

“Are you always this good at collecting strays?”

“Only the ones who make jokes when they’re scared.”

The truth of it left me briefly speechless.

Greg’s smile faded into something less performative. “That was too personal. Sorry.”

“No. It was accurate.”

“Accurate can still be a little personal.”

“You’re allowed to notice things.”

He studied me for a moment, and something passed between us that was not yet attraction, not quite trust, but the first thin thread of both. “So are you,” he said.

The diner smelled like coffee, syrup, and old vinyl booths warmed by years of sunlight. Greg chose a table near the window. He did not sit across from me until I sat first. When the waitress came over, he ordered pancakes and coffee, then looked at me.

“Tea,” I said. “If they have anything that isn’t black.”

“They have a packet of lemon.”

“A true culinary adventure.”

“I’ll protect you from the danger.”

He ordered the tea with a solemnity that made me smile again. While I waited, Greg told me about the town in fragments. The best place to watch the sunset. The grocery store that had surprisingly good fruit. The fact that the beach was beautiful until the tide exposed a collection of objects nobody wanted to discuss.

He did not tell me about the Gems. He did not tell me about his son, or the wars, or the ways he had once run from one life because another seemed more honest. Maybe those stories would come later. Maybe they would not. For that evening, he was a man with a guitar and a generous supply of pancakes.

When my tea arrived, Greg pushed the little packet of lemon toward me. “There. Protected.”

I squeezed it into the cup. “I feel safer already.”

“That’s the power of citrus.”

The pancakes arrived stacked high, butter melting down the sides. I had not realized how hungry I was until the first bite. Greg pretended not to notice how quickly I ate. He simply slid the syrup closer and started telling a story about the time he played an outdoor festival where a raccoon stole his capo.

“Did you get it back?”

“No. But the raccoon had excellent timing.”

I laughed so hard I had to put my fork down. Greg leaned back, satisfied, like he had accomplished something important.

When the sky turned violet, my phone finally came alive with a charge. Messages waited for me. Some were worried. Some were angry. One was simply a string of question marks. I stared at them until the words blurred.

“You don’t have to answer tonight,” Greg said.

“I probably should.”

“Probably is a word people use when they want to turn a choice into a punishment.”

I looked up.

He shrugged, suddenly self-conscious. “I’ve used it a lot.”

The diner had emptied around me. Outside, the boardwalk lights flickered on one by one, little gold stars along the shore. Greg’s guitar rested in its case beside him. There was a softness in the way he watched the darkening ocean, a kind of practiced loneliness that did not feel like a threat.

“Do you play here often?” I asked.

“The boardwalk? Sometimes. The diner? Only when I’m trying to annoy the staff.”

“You could play somewhere with a stage.”

“I do.” He smiled. “But stages are for being listened to. This is for figuring out what I want to say.”

The words stayed with me while Greg walked me back to the motel. At the entrance, he handed over my suitcase and pointed down the street.

“Tomorrow morning, there’s a rental office above the laundromat. The landlord is grouchy but fair. Ask for Mara. Tell her Greg sent you.”

“Will that help?”

“It might. If it doesn’t, tell her I sent you twice.”

“And if the curtains attack?”

“Call me.”

He pulled a business card from his pocket. It was bent at one corner and printed with a cartoonish drawing of a car. On the back, he wrote a number in thick black ink.

“You don’t have to call,” he added. “No pressure. I mean it.”

I folded the card carefully and put it in my wallet. “I might.”

“I’m very good at maybe,” he reminded me.

The door began to close behind me. Before it did, I looked back at him. Greg stood beneath the motel sign, silver hair bright in the fluorescent light, hands tucked into his pockets as if he did not want to make leaving harder.

“Greg?”

“Yeah?”

“Thank you for the pancakes.”

His smile returned, slow and warm. “Anytime.”

I carried my suitcase into the room. The curtains remained harmless. The bed was lumpy. The air conditioner made a rattling sound that suggested it had secrets. Still, when I placed the business card on the nightstand, the room felt a fraction less temporary.

Outside, somewhere beyond the buildings, a guitar began to play.

The melody was unfinished. It wandered, paused, and found its way forward anyway.

bridge_intro: The western footpath of the Lanternweald reached a pier that smelled of salt even when no sea was visible beyond it. At Starwake Pier, seashell wind chimes hung beside a doorway painted with little stars. Music drifted through the threshold in snatches, as if the air were rehearsing a song it had not finished yet. I followed it toward a boardwalk in another world. The people there were living lives, not acting out a story for me, and I had learned not to assume any door opened for my benefit alone. Still, I was curious enough to step through and find out who was playing.
